content: Immunization during pregnancy, which involves administering vaccines to pregnant women, is not a routine practice. This is because it is generally preferred to vaccinate women either before conception or after delivery. When widespread vaccination programs are in place, the likelihood of an unvaccinated pregnant woman being exposed to a vaccine-preventable infection is low. This often allows routine vaccinations to be postponed until the postpartum period. However, immunization during pregnancy may occur unintentionally or may be recommended in specific situations. In such cases, vaccination is considered prudent to reduce the risk of a particular disease for a pregnant woman or her fetus if there is a potential exposure. As a general rule, live virus or bacterial vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy. Live Attenuated Virus Vaccines The administration of live attenuated virus vaccines is generally contraindicated during pregnancy. This includes vaccines for measles, mumps, poliomyelitis, rubella, yellow fever, and varicella. It is important to note that there is no confirmed evidence of fetal harm resulting from the inadvertent administration of these vaccines during pregnancy. Additionally, no cases of congenital rubella syndrome have been reported when the rubella vaccine was unintentionally given during pregnancy. The MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine can be safely administered during lactation without affecting the baby. The CDC recommends that non-pregnant women who receive the MMR or varicella vaccine wait at least four weeks before attempting to conceive. Inactivated or Assembled Virus Vaccines Inactivated virus vaccines or vaccines containing viral components are generally not contraindicated during pregnancy. For example, influenza vaccination is recommended for pregnant women at risk, as are vaccines for hepatitis A and B. However, data on the safety of rabies vaccination during pregnancy are very limited. The HPV vaccine, which was recently introduced, is not indicated for use during pregnancy. While no adverse effects on the fetus have been reported, experience with the vaccine in pregnancy is limited, and any inadvertent administration during pregnancy should be reported to the CDC. Live Attenuated Bacterial Vaccines The BCG vaccine, which is used to prevent tuberculosis, is contraindicated during pregnancy. Inactivated Bacterial Vaccines Inactivated bacterial vaccines may be used during pregnancy for women who are at specific risk of exposure to certain infections. Vaccines against pneumococcal and meningococcal infections, as well as typhoid fever, have not been associated with confirmed adverse effects on the fetus, although data are limited. Similarly, data on anthrax vaccination during pregnancy are very limited but do not show any confirmed effects on the fetus. Toxoids Tetanus toxoids are considered safe for use during pregnancy. Immune Globulins Immune globulins are used for post-exposure prophylaxis and have not been associated with any reports of fetal harm. These agents are considered for use in pregnant women exposed to hepatitis B, rabies, tetanus, varicella, and hepatitis A. For the most current information on vaccination during pregnancy, healthcare providers and patients are encouraged to consult the CDC.
